newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: World trade ministers compromise on labour rights.
newsitem.headline: World trade ministers compromise on labour rights.

text.p: World trade ministers compromised at the eleventh hour on Thursday over the vexed question of whether the World Trade Organisation (WTO) should be involved in improving standards for workers, officials said.
They said the ministers had agreed to include a mention of labour rights, the most contentious issue at the WTO's five-day ministerial conference, in its final declaration on Friday.
"The labour issue is in the final declaration," a senior negotiator said.
Earlier Pakistan had declared victory in the battle to keep the issue out of the declaration winding up the WTO's first ministerial conference.
But Pakistani Commerce Minister Mohammed Zubair Khan conceded later that it would be mentioned.
That would be a victory for the United States, which conference sources said had threatened to block the declaration unless it was mentioned.

Washington argued that a key part of human rights had to be mentioned in connection with world trade, aware of rising concern at home about sweatshops and 250 million child workers, mostly in the developing world.
But senior officials from developing nations which fought a bitter battle to keep the issue out of the declaration said they had won too.

Countries like Pakistan, India and Malaysia, which led the developing world's battle, argued that the push to link labour rights and trade was merely a disguised attempt to use the WTO court to undermine their low-cost labour advantage.
They wanted it made clear that the International Labour Organisation (ILO), which was set up to deal with labour standards, was the right place for the issue and the WTO had no role.
Senior Indian official Tejendra Khanna said these countries wanted to keep the issue out of the declaration because they saw no relationship between labour rights and trade.

"Some say that even if this is the case, it's better to get it endorsed and so mandated by the ministers that these issues are not related and therefore there should not be further reference to them at the WTO," Khanna told reporters.
"People are saying if we can find satisfactory language that can express that definitively, perhaps we will be able to go along," he said.
Conference sources said it was evident that even the most ardent hold-outs in the developing world had finally come round to that idea.

They said the final declaration would refer to the ILO as "the competent body" to set and promote good labour standards and that the ILO and the WTO would "continue their existing collaboration" on the issue.
It would specifically "reject the use of labour standards for protectionist purposes," they said.
The ministers would also declare that they "agree that the comparative advantage of countries, particularly developing countries, must be in no way put into question," the sources said.
The International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), which claims 124 affiliate members in 136 countries, applauded the compromise but said the debate was more important than the outcome.
"What is significant is that the ministers now know that the issue of labour standards and trade is here to stay and cannot be swept under the carpet," it said in a statement.
